subject: Polity
description: Article 52-78 — election, executive, legislative, judicial, financial, emergency powers; vetoes

questions.stem: The President of India is elected by an Electoral College consisting of:

options.option_text: Elected members of both Houses of Parliament + elected members of State Legislative Assemblies + elected members of UT Assemblies of Delhi & Puducherry
All members of all State Legislatures

questions.explanation: Article 54 — Electoral College for President: ELECTED members of (i) both Houses of Parliament (Lok Sabha + Rajya Sabha), (ii) all State Legislative Assemblies, (iii) Legislative Assemblies of UTs of Delhi & Puducherry (added by 70th Amendment, 1992). Nominated members do NOT vote. Elected by single transferable vote, secret ballot, proportional representation. Value of MLA's vote = (state population / total elected MLAs in state) / 1000. MP's vote value = total MLA value / total elected MPs.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The 'Pocket Veto' — never used by any President but is most associated with President Zail Singh in 1986 — refers to:

options.option_text: Indefinite withholding of assent — neither signing nor returning the bill
Sending a bill to the Supreme Court

questions.explanation: Pocket Veto — President neither signs the bill, nor returns it, nor refuses assent. The Constitution sets no time-limit for the President to act on an ordinary bill, so it can be 'put in the pocket' indefinitely. Zail Singh used it on the Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill, 1986 — bill never became law. Other vetoes — Absolute Veto (refuse assent), Suspensive Veto (return for reconsideration; if Parliament passes again, must assent), Qualified Veto (does NOT exist in India — it's a US concept where a 2/3 majority over-rides).

questions.stem: Under Article 72, the President can grant pardon, reprieve, respite, remission of punishment OR suspension — including for which case-type that the Governor cannot pardon?

options.option_text: Death sentence and Court Martial cases

questions.explanation: Two crucial differences between Article 72 (President) and Article 161 (Governor): (i) President can pardon DEATH sentences; Governor cannot. (ii) President can pardon Court-Martial sentences; Governor cannot. The Governor's pardoning power is restricted to offences against State laws (matters in the State List). Both can grant Pardon, Commutation, Remission, Respite, Reprieve. President's pardoning is exercised on aid and advice of the Cabinet (Maru Ram, 1980; Kehar Singh, 1989; Epuru Sudhakar, 2006).
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: An ordinance issued by the President under Article 123 must be approved by Parliament within:

options.option_text: 30 days from the start of the next session
6 weeks from the start of the next session — else it lapses

questions.explanation: Article 123(2)(a) — an ordinance ceases to operate on the expiration of 6 weeks from the reassembly of Parliament. So effective maximum life = 6 months (max recess) + 6 weeks ≈ 7.5 months. Ordinances can be made only when Parliament is not in session and the President is satisfied immediate action is necessary. Subject to judicial review (D.C. Wadhwa, 1987 — re-promulgation without legislative approval struck down). Krishna Kumar Singh (2017) reaffirmed parliamentary supremacy over ordinance-making.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Which of the following bills CANNOT be returned by the President for reconsideration?

options.option_text: Both Money Bill and Constitution Amendment Bill

questions.explanation: Two bill-types where the President has NO suspensive veto: (1) Money Bills (Art 110) — already moved with President's prior recommendation, so returning is illogical; President must either assent or withhold (in practice always assents). (2) Constitution Amendment Bills — after the 24th Amendment (1971), Article 368 mandates that the President 'shall give assent' to a Constitution Amendment Bill duly passed; no return option. Ordinary bills under Art 111 can be returned once.

questions.stem: The President of India is the 'Supreme Commander' of the Indian Armed Forces under which Article?
questions.explanation: Article 53(2) — 'The supreme command of the Defence Forces of the Union shall be vested in the President and the exercise thereof shall be regulated by law.' This is a CEREMONIAL command — actual operational command rests with the Chiefs and the Defence Ministry under the political head (PM via Cabinet). The President appoints Chiefs of Army, Navy, Air Force; the CDS is appointed by the Cabinet's Appointments Committee.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The 42nd Constitutional Amendment (1976) made it explicit that the President shall act:

options.option_text: On his own discretion in all matters
In accordance with the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers
Only on the advice of the Supreme Court
Only on the advice of the Prime Minister, no Cabinet

questions.explanation: Article 74(1), as amended by the 42nd Amendment (1976) and 44th Amendment (1978), reads — 'There shall be a Council of Ministers with the Prime Minister at the head to aid and advise the President who shall, in the exercise of his functions, act in accordance with such advice.' The 44th Amendment added a proviso allowing the President to send back the advice ONCE for reconsideration; if returned with the same advice, must accept. Pre-1976 it was implicit; the 42nd Amendment made it textually binding.
